explanations.explanation: That's the word. He says, “…save me, that I may keep Your testimonies.” He wants the rescue, and he wants to keep God's testimonies once he has it. I think that's a man who plans to stay put on the right path, not just get out of the mess.

Teach is a good word, and it does show up later in this psalm. Down in verse 171 he says, “…for You teach me Your statutes.” But in verse 146 he asks to be saved so he may keep God's testimonies. In this verse, he's the one doing the keeping.

Defend is in this passage too, but it's a different request. In verse 154 he asks God, “Defend my cause and redeem me…” That's something he asks God to do for him. Here in verse 146 he's talking about what he wants to do, which is keep God's testimonies.
Yes, ma'am, yes, sir. He says, “…in Your word I have put my hope.” Notice what he does before dawn. He cries for help, and then he puts his hope in the word. That's where he lands every time.

I see why you'd go there, since he's up before dawn. But the verse never says he hopes in the morning light. He says, “…in Your word I have put my hope.” He's up before the sun, so the sun isn't what he's counting on.

Nope, and the verse gives it away. A man who rises before dawn and cries for help isn't bragging about his own muscles, I think. He says, “…in Your word I have put my hope.” His hope sits in God's word, not in himself.

That's it. He says his eyes anticipate the watches of night, “that I may meditate on Your word.” So the night isn't just something he stays up through. He looks ahead to it because he wants that time with the word. I think that's a man who wants more hours with God's word, not fewer.

explanations.answer: To keep watch over the city
explanations.explanation: The word watches might make you think of a guard on a wall. But this verse never mentions a city or a guard. It says his eyes anticipate the watches of night “that I may meditate on Your word.” The reason is the word itself.

He does have enemies in this psalm, and he talks about them plenty. But in verse 148 the stated purpose is different. He says, “…that I may meditate on Your word.” His eyes are on the word, not on his enemies.

I get why that sounds possible, since they're drawing near. But the verse closes the door. It says, “Those who follow after wickedness draw near; they are far from Your law.” So they're close to the writer, but they're far from God's law.
That's the one. They draw near to the writer, but verse 150 says they “are far from Your law.” They're close in one direction and far in the other. That's some very impressive distance management.

Yep. He says, “You are near, O LORD, and all Your commandments are true.” Notice he says it right when the wicked are drawing near. He sets that next to the fact that God is near. I think that's a man who knows where to look when the crowd gets close.

Heavy is how a tray of dough feels at 6 a.m., but it's not what the writer says. His word for the commandments is true. He says, “You are near, O LORD, and all Your commandments are true.” Nothing in that verse weighs them down.

Hidden would sound strange next to what he says in the same breath. He says, “You are near, O LORD…” and then calls all the commandments true. Nobody describes something hidden and near in the same sentence. The word he uses is true.

The verse says otherwise. He writes, “Long ago I learned from Your testimonies that You have established them forever.” Long ago is the key. This isn't a fresh discovery. It's something he learned a good while back.
Right. Verse 152 says, “Long ago I learned from Your testimonies that You have established them forever.” That's not last week's news. He's been standing on this one for a long time.

explanations.answer: He has not forgotten God's law
explanations.explanation: Yes. He says, “Look upon my affliction and rescue me, for I have not forgotten Your law.” That's the reason he gives. He doesn't list his good deeds or his history. He just says he hasn't forgotten the law.

You'd expect that from somebody in affliction, and I wouldn't blame him. But he never says it. The reason in the verse is, “…for I have not forgotten Your law.” He doesn't count up his suffering at all.

explanations.answer: He was born in God's land
explanations.explanation: That one never comes up in this passage. He doesn't mention where he was born at all. His reason is, “…for I have not forgotten Your law.” It's about what he holds onto, not where he comes from.

Correct. He says, “Salvation is far from the wicked because they do not seek Your statutes.” Pay attention to the reason he gives. It's the not seeking. That's the contrast he's drawing with himself, since he's up before dawn seeking.

That's what the verse says, though. Verse 155 reads, “Salvation is far from the wicked because they do not seek Your statutes.” The writer says it plainly, with the reason right there in the same line.
Not quite. The verse says the opposite. He says, “Though my persecutors and foes are many, I have not turned from Your testimonies.” Many foes, and he's still facing the same direction.

That's it. He says, “Though my persecutors and foes are many, I have not turned from Your testimonies.” That word though matters. Lots of people against him, and he doesn't turn. It would be easy to say they'd wear him down, but the verse says otherwise.

That's the one. He says, “Consider how I love Your precepts, O LORD; give me life according to Your loving devotion.” He points to his love for the precepts. Then he asks for life according to God's loving devotion.

He does talk about waiting later, in verse 166, where he says he waits for God's salvation. But in verse 159 he's asking God to consider something else. He says, “Consider how I love Your precepts, O LORD…” That's the thing he puts forward.
That one's not in the verse at all. He doesn't hand God a list of his hard work. He says, “Consider how I love Your precepts, O LORD…” What he puts forward is his love, not his effort.
Yes. Verse 160 says, “The entirety of Your word is truth…” Entirety means the whole thing. Not a favorite chapter or a few good verses. He means every bit of it.
Most sounds humble, but it's not what he says. The verse reads, “The entirety of Your word is truth…” Entirety doesn't leave any leftovers. That's the whole batch, with no crumbs set aside.

That would make his claim a whole lot smaller. But he says, “The entirety of Your word is truth…” He doesn't limit it to what he's learned so far. The whole word is truth, whether he's read it all or not.
That's it. He says, “Rulers persecute me without cause, but my heart fears only Your word.” Rulers are on one side, and God's word is on the other. His heart has only one thing it fears.

Anger might fit with rulers coming after him. But the verse doesn't say that. It reads, “Rulers persecute me without cause, but my heart fears only Your word.” Rulers are the ones persecuting him, and the word is what he fears.
Hand shows up in this passage, but in a different spot. In verse 173 he asks, “May Your hand be ready to help me…” Verse 161 is about what his heart fears, and the verse says it's “only Your word.”
Yes. He says, “I rejoice in Your promise like one who finds great spoil.” That's a joy you can picture, someone coming across a big find. And his find is God's promise.

explanations.answer: Someone who wins a long race
explanations.explanation: A race win is a joyful picture, I'll give you that. But the writer doesn't use it. He says, “I rejoice in Your promise like one who finds great spoil.” There's no finish line here, just a find.
That's a happy picture too, but it's not the one in the verse. He says, “I rejoice in Your promise like one who finds great spoil.” Finding great spoil is the comparison he picks.
Yep. Verse 164 says, “Seven times a day I praise You for Your righteous judgments.” That's a lot of praise in one day. I'm out here with flour on my mustache and I can't keep up with that.
Three is a fine number, but it's not what the verse says. He says, “Seven times a day I praise You for Your righteous judgments.” Seven, not three. He's well past a morning, noon and night routine.
Twelve would be even more, and I'd have to sit down. But the verse says, “Seven times a day I praise You for Your righteous judgments.” The number is seven.

I'd have guessed that too, but the verse says otherwise. It reads, “Abundant peace belongs to those who love Your law; nothing can make them stumble.” Nothing means nothing. That's a pretty big promise.

That's right. Verse 165 says, “Abundant peace belongs to those who love Your law; nothing can make them stumble.” Not a small thing, not a medium thing, nothing. It's right there next to the abundant peace.

Yes. He says, “I obey Your precepts and Your testimonies, for all my ways are before You.” The word for ties the obeying to his ways being before God. I think that's a man who knows he's never out of God's sight, and he lives like it.
The verse actually says it. He writes, “I obey Your precepts and Your testimonies, for all my ways are before You.” So he obeys, and he gives that reason in the same line. Nothing here to flip.

That's the one. He says, “May my cry come before You, O LORD; give me understanding according to Your word.” He's not asking for a pile of stuff. He wants to understand, and he wants it according to God's word.
Riches would be nice, but he doesn't ask for them. His request is, “…give me understanding according to Your word.” He wants understanding, and nothing in the verse mentions money.
He does have a lot of foes in this psalm, so victory would make sense. But he doesn't ask for it here. In verse 169 he says, “…give me understanding according to Your word.” That's his request.

Yes. Verse 171 says, “My lips pour forth praise, for You teach me Your statutes.” The praise pours out because God teaches him. I'd say a lot of us could use a mouth like that before our first coffee.
It's right there in the verse, though. He says, “My lips pour forth praise, for You teach me Your statutes.” Praise pours out and God's teaching is the reason he gives. Pretty plain.
Yes. He says, “May Your hand be ready to help me, for I have chosen Your precepts.” He didn't just land on them. He chose them, and that's the reason he gives for asking for help.
Inherited would mean they were handed down to him, and the verse doesn't say that. It reads, “May Your hand be ready to help me, for I have chosen Your precepts.” He's the one who chose.
Questioned is the opposite of the tone in this verse. He says, “May Your hand be ready to help me, for I have chosen Your precepts.” He chose them, and that's his reason. No second-guessing here.
That's it. Verse 175 says, “Let me live to praise You; may Your judgments sustain me.” He wants to live so that he can praise. Right back to where this psalm started, with his mouth full of praise.
He does mention his foes in this psalm, so it's a fair guess. But verse 175 doesn't say that. It reads, “Let me live to praise You…” Praise is the reason he gives for wanting to live.
That sounds lovely, but he doesn't ask for it here. The verse says, “Let me live to praise You; may Your judgments sustain me.” Praise is what he wants to live for.

explanations.answer: He has strayed like a lost sheep
explanations.explanation: Yes. The psalm ends, “I have strayed like a lost sheep; seek Your servant, for I have not forgotten Your commandments.” He says it plainly about himself. And then he asks to be sought.

explanations.answer: He has stood like a strong tower
explanations.explanation: A strong tower would be a big finish, but it's not what he says. He ends with, “I have strayed like a lost sheep…” For his last word about himself, he picks a lost sheep. He doesn't brag at all.

explanations.answer: He has run like a swift deer
explanations.explanation: A swift deer sounds impressive, but the psalm doesn't end there. The last verse says, “I have strayed like a lost sheep; seek Your servant…” He doesn't run off a hero. He asks to be sought.
